default.q.test-1-q1-1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) かけ
The structure V-ます stem + かけ describes an action that has been started but remains unfinished. Here, the book is still only partly read: 読みかけ.
default.q.test-1-q1-1.explanation: The structure 「V-ます (remove ます) + かけ」 describes an action that has only just begun or is still halfway complete. The complete dialogue means: A: “May I borrow the book that’s here for a little while?” — B: “Oh, I’m still in the middle of reading that one.” Related example: 「テーブルの上に飲みかけのジュースが置いてある。」 (“There is a half-finished glass of juice on the table.”) For the N2 exam, remember that 「〜かけ」 means “unfinished” or “halfway done,” in contrast to 「〜きる」, which means completing something entirely. Do not confuse it with 「〜がち」, which indicates a tendency or a recurring undesirable state.

default.q.test-1-q1-1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「きり」usually follows V-た and indicates that a situation has continued unchanged since an event occurred; it is not used to indicate an unfinished action.
default.q.test-1-q1-1.why.2: ✓ (c) 「〜かけ」combines with the verb stem formed by removing ます from the ます-form (読みかけ) to express an action that has been started but remains unfinished.
default.q.test-1-q1-1.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜がち」 follows V-ます with ます removed, or a noun, to indicate a tendency to occur frequently, usually negatively. It is not appropriate in this context.
default.q.test-1-q10-10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) からといって
The grammar pattern 「〜からといって」 means “even if one takes ... as a reason, that does not mean one may/should ...,” which fits the advisory or cautionary clause that follows.
default.q.test-1-q10-10.explanation: The pattern 「plain form + からといって」 means “just because...” or “it does not follow that...”. It is used to reject the assumption that the reason in the preceding clause automatically justifies an action or belief. The following clause often contains a negative or advisory expression such as 〜わけではない, 〜とは限らない, or 〜よくない. The complete sentence means: “Even if it is because of the hot weather, drinking only cold beverages is not good for your health.” Compare: 日本に住んでいるからといって、日本語が上手に話せるとは限らない (“Just because someone lives in Japan does not necessarily mean they can speak Japanese well.”). When solving questions, check the following clause: if it contains a negative expression or warning about a bad consequence, think of 「〜からといって」. Do not confuse it with 「くせに」, which is used to express sarcasm or criticism toward a specific person’s behavior.
default.q.test-1-q10-10.why.0: ✗ (a) くせに is used to criticize or sarcastically point out contradictory behavior or qualities of the same subject, so it does not fit a context involving general advice.
default.q.test-1-q10-10.why.1: ✗ (b) ついでに means “while doing A, take the opportunity to do B”; it does not express a cause-and-effect relationship.
default.q.test-1-q10-10.why.2: ✓ (c) からといって combines with the plain form to express “even if the reason is that it is hot, ...,” flowing naturally into the conclusion 「冷たいものばかり飲むのは体によくない」.
default.q.test-1-q10-10.why.3: ✗ (d) だけでなく means “not only... but also...,” and is used to add parallel information, not in this conditional-evaluative sentence pattern.
default.q.test-1-q11-11.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) からこそ
This structure emphasizes the fundamental reason and means “precisely because…,” fitting the decisive reason that enables the speaker to enjoy working.
default.q.test-1-q11-11.explanation: The structure 「〜からこそ」combines with the plain form (V/A-i/A-naだ/Nだ) to strongly emphasize the sole or most important reason: "precisely because..." The following clause often expresses a feeling, positive evaluation, or ability and frequently ends with 「〜のだ」, 「〜わけだ」, or 「〜できる」. The complete sentence means: "It is precisely because I have trustworthy coworkers that I am able to enjoy my work." Compare: 家族の支えがあるからこそ、困難を乗り越えることができた。("It was precisely because I had my family's support that I was able to overcome the difficulties.") When the first clause states an essential condition and the second expresses a positive result with 「〜のだ」, choose 「からこそ」.

default.q.test-1-q11-11.why.1: ✗ (b) The phrase 「からさえ」is not a standard structure for expressing an emphasized cause-and-effect relationship in this context.
default.q.test-1-q11-11.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern 「にしたがって」 expresses a corresponding change (“the more... the more...”) or following a rule; it does not indicate a reason.
default.q.test-1-q11-11.why.3: ✗ (d) 「に加えて」 means “in addition to” or “besides” and adds information; it is not used to explain a cause.

✅ Correct answer: (c) からには
The pattern 「〜からには」 means “now that...” or “once...,” and the following clause often expresses an appeal, determination, or obligation. It fits the exhortational ending 「〜頑張ろう」 perfectly.
default.q.test-1-q12-12.explanation: The pattern 「Plain form (most commonly V-る / V-た) + からには」 means “once...,” or “now that...,” and is used when the speaker expresses determination, responsibility, or a strong appeal in the following clause. The ending often takes forms such as 〜よう, 〜べきだ, or 〜てください. The complete sentence means: “Now that we have discussed it repeatedly and reached a decision together, let us do our best to achieve success.” Compare this example: 「約束したからには、最後までやり遂げるべきだ。」(Once you have made a promise, you should carry it through to the end.) In similar N2 grammar questions, remember that the equivalent Japanese pattern is 「〜上は」 or 「〜以上は」; the combined form 「〜うえには」 does not exist as shown in choice (a). Also, 「〜ためには」 does not combine with the past form to express purpose, and 「〜わけには」 must always be followed by 「いかない」.

default.q.test-1-q12-12.why.1: ✗ (b) When「〜ためには」expresses purpose, it does not combine with the past-form verb「決めた」before it.
default.q.test-1-q12-12.why.2: ✓ (c) 「V-た＋からには」means that once a decision has been made, one must do one’s utmost, and it combines correctly with the invitation「〜頑張ろう」in the following clause.
default.q.test-1-q12-12.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜わけには」 is an incomplete connective form, normally appearing in the complete predicate structure 「〜わけにはいかない」 at the end of a sentence.

It means that, right in the middle or at the height of an ongoing action, an unexpected event interrupts and causes difficulty. In context, the complete sentence means: “An earthquake occurred while I was watching a movie, and it frightened me terribly.” Example: 「重要な会議を行っている最中に、停電が起きた。」 (A power outage occurred in the middle of an important meeting.) As a memory aid, 「最中」 means the very middle of a time period, so the preceding action must be ongoing and use 「V-ている」; do not use the dictionary form 「V-る」 or past form 「V-た」.

default.q.test-1-q13-13.why.3: ✓ (d) This is correct because the grammar pattern 「最中」must be used with the progressive form 「V-ている」to describe an action in progress when it is interrupted.
default.q.test-1-q14-14.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) くせに
This pattern expresses a contrast between two contradictory behaviors by the same person. It clearly conveys dissatisfaction and criticism toward someone who is lenient with themselves but strict with others.
default.q.test-1-q14-14.explanation: The pattern 「plain form (A-na + な / N + の) + くせに」means “even though / despite,” and expresses dissatisfaction, sarcasm, or criticism toward two contrasting attitudes or behaviors of the same subject. The complete sentence means: “That person is always lenient about their own mistakes, yet is extremely strict about other people’s errors.” Another example is: 「何も知らないくせに、偉そうに指図しないでよ。」(You don’t know anything, so don’t order people around as if you were important.) Unlike the conjunction 「のに」, which can express neutral surprise or regret, 「くせに」always carries a negative, critical nuance and should not be used for the speaker’s own behavior.

default.q.test-1-q14-14.why.2: ✗ (c) せいで expresses a negative cause-and-effect relationship (“because of / due to...”), and is not used to express the contrast between two attitudes shown in the question.
default.q.test-1-q14-14.why.3: ✗ (d) からには means “once... then one must/will...,” and is generally used to express determination or a moral obligation, not merely contrast.

Compare: 「いろいろ悩んだ末に、転職することを決意した。」(After much agonizing, I decided to change jobs.) Clues include expressions indicating extended time or effort, such as 「長時間」, 「散々」, and 「いろいろ」. Also distinguish it from the similar pattern 「〜あげく」, which generally leads to a negative or regrettable outcome.

✅ Correct answer: (c) くらいだった
The pattern 「〜くらいだ」 changes to the past form 「〜くらいだった」 to describe how extremely busy someone was in the past when overwhelmed with work.

The form「〜もないくらいだ」often emphasizes that not even the minimum amount is available or possible. The complete sentence means: “When I was young, I was so consumed by work that I did not have even a little time for life at home.” Compare:「昨日は足が痛くて、一歩も歩けないくらいだった。」(Yesterday my feet hurt so much that I could not walk even one step.) When a past time expression such as「若い頃は」appears with the emphatic「〜もない」, choose the past degree form「〜くらいだった」rather than present-tense conjectural endings such as「〜でしょう」or「〜だろう」.

default.q.test-1-q16-16.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜ことはない」 means that something is unnecessary or impossible; it is not used to express the degree of a state that has already occurred.
default.q.test-1-q16-16.why.2: ✓ (c) 「〜くらいだった」 combines with 「〜もない」 in the preceding clause to express an extreme degree in the past: being so busy that there was not even enough time to stay at home.
default.q.test-1-q16-16.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜はずはなかった」expresses the firm judgment that something could not have happened in the past, so it does not fit a sentence expressing degree.

✅ Correct answer: (b) さえあれば
The structure「N + さえ〜ば」means “as long as there is/are …, that is enough to ….” It fits the speaker’s wish that having only enough free time would guarantee a trip to Kyoto to see the autumn leaves.
default.q.test-1-q17-17.explanation: The key pattern 「N + さえ + conditional form (〜ば/なら/たら)」means “as long as the minimum condition is met.” Here, 休み combines with the affirmative conditional あれば to express the wish to travel if there is a break. The complete dialogue means: A: “Look at this news article. default.q.test-1-q17-17.why.3: ✗ (d) The combination 「こそなければ」does not form a conditional pattern meaning “as long as,” and its negative meaning is also completely unsuitable.

✅ Correct answer: (a) 戻り次第
The pattern 「V-ます stem + 次第」 means “as soon as...” and expresses the intention to carry out a purposeful action immediately after the preceding action is completed.
default.q.test-1-q18-18.explanation: The pattern 「Vます (ます removed) + 次第 (しだい)」 is commonly used in formal or business language to mean that action B will be carried out immediately after event A is completed. The complete dialogue means: A says, "I would like to speak with Mr. Tanaka for a moment..." B replies, "I’m very sorry, but Mr. Tanaka has just stepped away from his desk. Shall I ask him to call you back as soon as he returns?" Another example: 「詳細が決まり次第、メールでご連絡いたします。」(I will contact you by email as soon as the details have been decided.) 「次第」 commonly follows verbs indicating a point of completion or arrival, such as 戻る, 着く, and 決まる, and the following clause expresses the speaker’s intention. It differs completely from the simultaneous action expressed by 「～ながら」 or the manner expressed by 「～とおり」.

default.q.test-1-q18-18.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「～とおり」means “just as” or “according to,” and is not used to indicate the chronological sequence of events.
default.q.test-1-q18-18.why.2: ✗ (c) The structure「～ままに」means “just as / leaving something to...,” and is completely unsuitable in the context of arranging a time to call back.

✅ Correct answer: (b) だけあって
The structure 「〜だけあって」 combines naturally with the adverb 「さすが」 to emphasize that the excellent food and service are fully worthy of the restaurant’s reputation.

It often occurs with the adverb 「さすが」. The complete sentence means: “As expected of a famous restaurant, both the food and the service are excellent.” Compare: 「彼は10年も日本に住んでいるだけあって、日本語がとても流暢だ。」(He has lived in Japan for 10 years, so it is no wonder that he speaks Japanese so fluently.) default.q.test-1-q19-19.why.1: ✓ (b) The pattern 「〜だけあって」 means “as expected of / true to the reputation of,” and, together with 「さすが」, expresses a result that fully lives up to the reputation.
default.q.test-1-q19-19.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern 「〜ばかりでなく」 means “not only... but also,” and does not fit the context or sentence structure when placed after the noun to connect the ideas.
default.q.test-1-q19-19.why.3: ✗ (d) The pattern 「〜としたら」 means “if” or “supposing that,” and is not used to affirm a fact while adding praise.

The complete sentence means: “While taking my friend to the station, I stopped at the supermarket in front of the station to do some shopping before coming home.” A comparative example is: 「コンビニに行くついでに、ゴミを出してきた。」(While going to the convenience store, I took out the trash.) To solve this type of question, find the V-る/V-た verb that comes immediately before 「ついでに」. This helps identify the main action serving as the premise and the additional action performed along the way.

default.q.test-9-q1-1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「駅前のスーパーで」 in position 4 indicates the location where the shopping action 「買い物をしてきた」 in the following clause took place.
default.q.test-9-q1-1.why.2: ✓ (c) ついでに is in the third position, marked with an asterisk (*), and combines with 「送って行った」 to connect the main action with an additional action performed along the way.
default.q.test-9-q1-1.why.3: ✗ (d) The verb 「送って行った」 occupies the second position, completing the main action clause 「駅まで送って行った」 before 「ついでに」.

A similar example expressing emotion is: 「一人暮らしを始めたばかりで、寂しくてしょうがない。」 (I have just started living alone, so I feel terribly lonely).

default.q.test-9-q3-3.explanation: The N2 grammar pattern「～だけあって」combines with the plain form of a verb, adjective, or noun and means "just as one would expect from..." or "true to...." It expresses praise or appreciation for a result that fully matches the reason, experience, or qualifications stated in the preceding clause. The correct order is a → d → b → c:「大山さんは以前京都に住んでいただけあって、この地域のことをよく知っている。」(As one would expect from someone who used to live in Kyoto, Oyama knows this area very well.) To solve it, first pair the particle and verb「京都に住んでいた」, attach it to「だけあって」as the reason clause, then place the object phrase「この地域のことを」before the predicate「よく知っている」. Another example:「彼は毎日練習しているだけあって、ピアノがとても上手だ。」(As one would expect from someone who practices every day, he plays the piano very well.)

default.q.test-9-q6-6.explanation: The key grammar pattern is the reporting structure 「〜によれば…〜ということだ／とのことだ」. It usually follows a reliable information source and combines with a verb or adjective in 普通形 (plain form) to report information that has been heard. The particle 「が」 then creates a contrast between the reported information and reality. The completed sentence is: 「政府の発表によれば、景気は回復しているということだが、そうした実感はまだない。」 (“According to the government announcement, the economy is reportedly recovering, but I still do not have any real sense of it.”) Another example is: 「ニュースによれば、今年の夏は猛暑になるということだが、熱中症の対策は済んでいますか。」 (“According to the news, this summer is expected to be extremely hot. Have you taken measures against heatstroke?”) As a quick strategy, when 「〜によれば」 appears at the beginning, look for the corresponding reporting ending 「〜ということだ／そうだ」 with a verb in 普通形, then use the contrastive conjunction 「が」 to connect smoothly to the negative phrase 「まだない」 at the end.

Grammatically, 「本当だ」 connects with 「としても」 to form a concessive hypothetical clause, while 「この目で」 modifies 「確かめない」, which combines with 「かぎり」 to create the prerequisite condition leading to the negative result 「信じられない」. The complete sentence means: “Even if it is true, I still cannot believe it unless I confirm it with my own eyes.” Similar example: 実際に使ってみないかぎり、その良さはわかりません。 (“Unless you actually try using it, you cannot understand its advantages.”) Test-taking tip: When the sentence ends with a negative or impossibility expression such as 「信じられない」, quickly look for a verb in the nai-form that can combine with 「かぎり」 to form the prerequisite condition.
